This sociolinguistic profile summarizes the linguistic situation of the Korwa (ISO code [kfp]) and
Kodaku (ISO code [ksz]) languages spoken in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand states of India. The
purpose of the research was to assess the likelihood of need for vernacular language development.
The fieldwork was carried out in different phases, starting in June 2004, and completed by
September 2005. The tools used for the study were questionnaires, wordlists, recorded text tests, and
interviews. The results revealed that these languages would benefit from literature development in
view of ongoing language shift toward Sadri (ISO code [sck]), which is rapid in some segments of the
population and slow in other segments of the population. The report calls for efforts to revitalize

Language is always closely related to any society and people group. It is said to be a hallmark of their
identity. This sociolinguistic survey among the Korwa and Kodaku people of Chhattisgarh and
Jharkhand was initiated in response to a possible need for vernacular development. The primary
interest was to provide a clear idea about the sociolinguistic situation of Korwa and Kodaku for
likeminded people who are interested in language development. The research was carried out by
Gangadhar Behera, Jose P. Mathew, Binzy Joseph George, Liju Kuriakose, Sajayan V. Chacko, and
Symon George, beginning in mid-June 2004 to September 2005
As with its geographical diversity, India is extremely rich in languages, with languages falling
into four language families. The Chhota Nagpur plateau is a very good example of both the
geographical and the linguistic diversity in eastern India. It can be categorised as a multilingual
geographical setting in India. The plateau covers much of Jharkhand state as well as adjacent parts of
Orissa, Bihar, and Chhattisgarh. It is roughly situated between 22–24 degrees north latitude and 83–
85 degrees east longitude, which covers approximately 65,000 square kilometres. Much of this is
covered with tropical forest, predominantly with the Sal tree. The plateau is one of the few
remaining refuges left in India for tigers and Asian elephants (Wikipedia contributors 2022).
This area is home for many people groups, who speak languages belonging to the Austro-Asiatic,
Dravidian, and Indo-Aryan language families. Korwa and Kodaku are two tribes found in this region.
According to Singh (1994:545), in the notification list of Scheduled Tribes for Madhya Pradesh, the
Kodaku people have been grouped with the Korwa. However, Singh also mentions that, though the
Kodaku and Korwa are often grouped together, they have distinct identities of their own and are two

The Korwa people are said to be the original inhabitants of Korba and Surguja districts of
They were believed to be Zamindars (landlords) and Rajas (kings) who built forts and
were ruling the land. In the early 1900s, they were dubbed as the leaders and chiefs of this region
until powerful conquerors invaded them. For example, a king named Ghughus, belonging to the
Korwa community, ruled over Ratanpur. After that, the Rajputs took over the kingdom, and later this
was taken over by the British (Powercity Korba n.d.b). It is believed that during the British reign, the
Korwa kingdom was attacked and collapsed. According to the tales of the hills when the Korwa king
lost to the British, he along with his subjects fled to the jungles of Korea Jhadi (Korea hills)
The Korwa lived in and around the hills and forest for a long time, struggling for bare essentials
such as food, clothing, and shelter. Gradually this situation became the basis for their simple
lifestyle. This isolation forced them to develop their own means of survival. However, gradually their
isolation has been broken and so has their identity. As a result of their contact with the outside
world, their desire for further development is increasing (Mohan 1993:12–22).
Very little is known about the history of the Kodaku people. However, in the notification list of the
Scheduled Tribes in India, they have been grouped with the Korwa people (Singh 1994:545). Like the
Korwa people, the Kodaku people also consider themselves to be the successors of the Kauravs of
Mahabharata, and their lifestyle and culture are also comparable to that of the Pandos, a
neighbouring tribal group. They are a nomadic hill tribe, who earned their livelihood from the forest.
They used to clear the forests for seasonal cultivation, and others were getting the benefits of it.
However, gradually they began to live in the plains and were influenced by outsiders, especially by
Christian missionaries, who have helped them in different ways.
Both the Korwa and the Kodaku people are tribal communities who live an isolated life in the hills,
valleys, and forest regions. Access to their settlements by outsiders is often impossible. However, they
seem to be generally happy in their secluded lifestyle in their settlements. Both tribes are
distinguished from others by their isolated lifestyle and physical appearance. Generally they are short
in height with dark brown complexions (CTDP 2002:n.p.).
Their primary occupation is food-gathering and agriculture. Few of them possess cultivatable
land, but a major portion of it has been mortgaged to the neighbouring tribal and non-tribal
communities. Generally, they manage their livelihood by daily wage labour and selling collected
forest products in the local market (CTDP 2002:n.p.).
The women, besides attending to household
chores, take part in agricultural and non-agricultural labour.
The main staple of the Korwa and Kodaku is rice and wheat. They are not vegetarians. They eat
a variety of leafy vegetables and pulses. Drinking an indigenous alcohol, called
mahua flower and fermented rice, as well as smoking and chewing tobacco are among their habits.
They do not eat with other castes or tribes. However, they accept water and cooked food from
neighbours such as the Yadav, Bania, Gond, Kanwar, and Kharwar (Singh 1994:547).
There are no separate population figures available for the Korwa and Kodaku (Singh 1994:545).

21,940 in Jharkhand (Dubey 1987:486). By the 1991 census (RGCCI 1991) their population had

The Korwa people are mainly divided into two distinct groups, the Pahadi Korwa and the Dihari
Korwa. The ones who still live in the hills and forest are called Pahadi/Pahariya Korwa (‘hill
dwellers’) and the ones who came down and settled in the plain areas are called Dihari/Dihariya
Korwa (‘plains dwellers’). They are not mutually dependent on each other. Their lifestyle,
occupation, culture, etc. distinguish them as separate communities. The Dihari Korwa people live in a
village situation, while the Pahadi Korwa people usually live in the? hills and forests. Occupationally,
the Dihari Korwa people are agriculturists living in the plains, whereas the Pahadi Korwas people are
food gatherers and basket makers who live in the hills, usually covered by dense forests (Narayan
The Dihari Korwa people are developed farmers and economically stabilized, while the
Pahadi Korwa people are still economically poor.
In this study, the main focus is given to the Pahadi Korwa people group and their language.

Marriage is generally arranged through negotiation, by mutual consent. They mostly practise
monogamy; however polygamy is also practiced by some people. A bride price is required, which is
paid to the bride’s parents in cash and goods. One of the marriage rituals is to circle around the fire
five times. Divorce can be sought by either spouse on grounds of barrenness or adultery. There is no
bar for remarriage for either the man or the woman (Singh 1994:546).

Education was previously unattainable for both the Pahadi Korwa and the Kodaku people. Owing to
poverty, most of them are illiterate. Their children rarely studied beyond the primary school level.
According to various census reports, the literacy rate of the Pahadi Korwa people never exceeded 10

Now there is a deep awareness of the need for education among both people groups. The
government of Chhattisgarh has been extending educational facilities by opening hostels and schools
specifically for Pahadi Korwa children. At present, there are a few Pahadi Korwa students graduating
with degrees and representing their community in government offices. As for the Kodaku people, the
government does not extend much educational help, but different NGOs, especially Christian
missions, are providing educational facilities for them.

Language vitality is a key element in any sociolinguistic research. It deals with the life of the
language and its stability in succeeding generations. It relates to the overall strength of a language
and its perceived usefulness in a wide variety of situations. Many variables contribute to vitality,
such as patterns of language use and attitudes, native interest for language development, and the
status of a language in the larger society. The purpose of assessing language vitality in Korwa and
Kodaku is to throw light on the feasibility of language development (see Purpose, Goals, and
The study of language use patterns attempts to describe which languages or speech varieties
members of a community use in different social domains. These domains are contexts in which the
use of one language variety is considered more appropriate than another (Fasold 1984:183).
Similarly, the study of language attitudes generally deals with the perspectives people have toward a
language. It describes the feelings and preferences of people for their language as well as other
languages around them and shows the values they give to those particular languages. Ultimately,
subjects’ responses to questions concerning their language use patterns, attitudes (whether explicit or
unexpressed), and their interest in a language’s development give insight into the language vitality.
Their attitudes influence the results of efforts toward literacy and the acceptability of literature
The principal tool that was used for this study was a questionnaire on issues related to language
use, attitude, and vitality. These questions were administered to mother tongue speakers in different
villages. The subjects’ responses for each language are compiled. In addition, there were the informal
interviews held and the observations made during fieldwork. (See Appendix A.)

Among the Pahadi Korwa, a total of 61 subjects were questioned, from which two categories are
distinguished: those settlements where people speak Pahadi Korwa and those settlements where the
speakers are shifting from Pahadi Korwa to Sadri.
These categories were based on the overall
responses regarding language use and attitude within each settlement. The surveyors found that

Korwa people. The Korwa people there speak Sadri. The 15 respondents from this village are
categorised under Shifting Korwa. This segment of people has more contact with Sadri-speaking
people and has a positive attitude toward using Sadri. Moreover, in this settlement only one or two

Among Speaking Pahadi Korwa, the use of the mother tongue in community domains (such as
the home, with people of the same caste, children while playing, in marriage songs) is high. More
than three-quarters of the subjects (76–89%) reported that they use Korwa, their mother tongue, in
these domains. On the other hand, the LWC Sadri is used more in other domains, such as the market,
government offices, and in conversations with people from other castes.
Around one-quarter of the Pahadi Korwa subjects fall into the Shifting category. Respondents
from the Shifting Pahadi Korwa village reported using Sadri in all domains. Those who said they use
Korwa are mostly subjects who are 70–80 years old.

have comparatively more access to the outside world than those Pahadi Korwa still using Korwa as

the frequent use of Sadri and the fact that some Pahadi Korwa have already begun using Sadri almost

A couple of questions in relation to language use were administered in Kotagohna, a Dihari Korwa
village. Out of 19 subjects, all subjects reported that they widely use Sadri (or Surguja, an alternative
name). In fact, the respondents reported Sadri as their mother tongue, and that they use it in every
sphere of communication. A few respondents also stated that their children use Hindi in school. The
researchers’ observations also concur with the subjects’ responses that the Dihari Korwa people do
not have a separate mother tongue called Korwa.
Figure 1 shows the responses to language attitude questions except for one question which is
analysed separately below. Similar to the language use responses, the language attitude responses are
analysed separately according to villages speaking and shifting from Pahadi Korwa.
Figure 1. The language attitude responses among the Pahadi Korwa.
The attitude of the Speaking Pahadi Korwa subjects toward their mother tongue is very positive.
All of them said that they would like their children to read and write in the Korwa language. In
addition, most of them also believe that their language will continue to be used by the coming
generation. A little less than three-quarters of the subjects said that they would not be happy if their
children spoke only Hindi or Sadri. However, only 63 percent of them reported Korwa to be their
favourite language. Furthermore, when asked whether they allow marriage with a Pahadi Korwa
person who does not speak the Korwa language, most of them reported that such a marriage is
acceptable. However, they also expressed a desire that the person should be from the Korwa
community because they do not encourage marrying from outside their tribe. This reflects that the
mother tongue does not play an important role among the Pahadi Korwa in terms of their marriage
preferences and shows their flexibility toward their language.
The attitude of the Shifting Pahadi Korwa to the Korwa language seems to be strong only in the
case of vernacular education for their children. However, this response contradicts their language use
pattern in general: they use Sadri extensively in all domains. The respondents themselves regret not
being able to speak Korwa, but it is their desire that Korwa be taught to their children. With this in
mind, more than half of them expressed the expectation that their next generation would speak the
Korwa language, if someone would teach them. A little more than one-quarter of them are not happy
that their children speak only Sadri. Other responses reveal that the use of the Korwa language is not
at all important in marriage. All respondents reported that they would allow marriage with someone
whether they speak the Korwa language or not. Only 13 percent of them said that their favourite
language is Korwa, and this response was mostly from very old subjects. Overall, it is found that
while those who are no longer using Korwa retain a positive attitude toward language development,
Sadri is the preferred language in actual usage.
Apart from the above responses, other answers reflect the respondents’ attitudes toward their
language. A question, ‘If young people in your village did not speak Korwa, how would you feel?’,
was asked to both young and old subjects. Among Speaking Pahadi Korwa, most older subjects
expressed that they would be unhappy if their young people did not speak their language. Young
people also responded that older people feel bad if they do not speak the Korwa language. On the
other hand, when this same question was asked among Shifting Pahadi Korwa, the response suggest
that it does not bother the old people whether their young people speak the Korwa language or not.
In fact, one 80-year-old subject expressed that he is not sad for young people who are not able to
speak the Korwa language because he himself does not know how to speak the language. Overall

The question ‘What is your mother tongue, and did your forefathers have a different language than
what you speak today?’ was asked to find out whether the Dihari Korwa respondents perceive any
significant linguistic relation to Pahadi Korwa. All subjects reported Sadri to be their mother tongue,

The responses to the question ‘If young people in your village do not speak Sadri, how would

does not matter, however. Young subjects all felt that the old people would feel unhappy if they do

asked if the coming generations would continue to speak the language, all except one respondent
said that they will surely speak their mother tongue.

Therefore, it is always necessary to evaluate the bilingual proficiency of a community before

The place of Hindi and Sadri
Hindi, an Indo-Aryan language, is the national language of India and a lingua franca throughout
northern India. It is also the official language of some states in northern India. Hindi has a great
influence in India, except in some of the southernmost parts. There is a great amount of literature
available in Hindi. The media is also dominated by the use of Hindi. Overall, people like Hindi
because of its prestige and perceived “sweetness”. However, there are many local languages that are
preferred to Hindi in some regions, especially among the tribal areas in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.
Sadri, also an Indo-Aryan language, is spoken as a mother tongue by numerous Adivasi groups
and castes spread across India and Bangladesh. It also serves as a language of wider communication
in these areas (Abraham 1995:11). Although Chhattisgarhi is the state language of Chhattisgarh and
Hindi is the official language of both Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand (Hindi is, for example, the medium
for instruction in schools, and is used primarily for government purposes). Sadri has a great influence
in northern Chhattisgarh and southwestern Jharkhand. Tribes in these areas use Sadri more than
Hindi. As mentioned earlier, some of these tribes even speak Sadri as their first language (1995:13).
On the other hand, it is the second language of some tribes, especially tribes such as the Korwa and
the Kodaku, while Hindi is a third language.
The variety of Sadri spoken in Jharkhand and Orissa is being promoted and developed. People
often consider this variety to be the standard. Abraham (1995:11) reports that the language
development efforts in the Sadri language have been widespread; there is literature available in this
variety. Sadri speakers, as well as the researchers, reported seeing Sadri books, listening to Sadri
language cassettes and CDs, and hearing radio programs in Sadri. Books written in the Sadri
language include an English-Sadri dictionary (Blain 1975), religious books, history books, especially
developed in Jharsuguda or Rourkela, Orissa. There is a Sadri radio program which broadcasts from
Ranchi, Jharkhand. According to Masica (1991:442), “Sadri language development is expected to
continue. It is particularly active in Ranchi, Jharkhand, where the Sadri language is offered as a
subject at the University of Ranchi.” Furthermore, in this modern age, media (audio and video) have
played a significant role in propagating the wide use of Sadri. With these factors in mind, the
researchers determined they should investigate Sadri bilingualism rather than Hindi bilingualism.
For bilingualism testing, the primary method is the sentence repetition test (SRT). However, since a
Sadri SRT has not been developed, the researchers opted to use the RTT for exploring Sadri
bilingualism among Korwa and Kodaku speakers. An RTT, however, is used to discern the
intelligibility among related speech varieties. It is not a common method for testing bilingualism as it
cannot determine bilingual proficiency at higher levels; at the most, it can confirm low proficiency
levels. In addition to the RTT, a few questions regarding testees’ self-reported abilities in Sadri were
included as part of the post-RTT questionnaire. The researchers’ observations in the field also helped
to evaluate Sadri bilingualism levels among the Korwa and Kodaku groups.
An RTT can be used to provide a preliminary assessment of a community’s abilities in a second
language. The procedures for evaluating testees’ bilingual abilities using this method are the same as
those used for a dialect intelligibility testing. As this method only evaluates the comprehension
ability of simple narratives, it is not adequate for evaluating higher levels of bilingual proficiency
When an RTT is used for evaluating bilingualism, more subjects are tested compared with
intelligibility testing. But, in the case of this survey, the willingness of people to be tested was quite
low. Researchers spent considerable time explaining the purpose of the test. Some subjects demanded
money in exchange for being tested.
When conducting any test, care should be taken to test a sample that represents the
demographic characteristics of the community, namely men and women, young and old, and
educated and uneducated. However, in this survey, it was difficult to find a sufficient number of
subjects from each of these categories.

This description of RTT procedures is adapted from Rensch et al. (1992:153-156).
The extent to which speakers of related linguistic varieties understand one another can be
studied by means of tape-recorded texts. Such studies investigate whether speakers of one variety
understand a narrative text of another variety and are able to answer questions about the content of
that text. The accuracy with which subjects answer these questions is taken as an index of their
comprehension of that speech form. From the percentage of correct answers, the amount of
intelligibility between speech forms is inferred. The RTT procedures followed in this survey are based
on the procedures described in Casad (1974) and Blair (1990).
Short, personal experience narratives are deemed to be most suitable for recorded text testing in
that the content must be relatively unpredictable and the speech form should be natural. Folklore or
other material thought to be widely known is avoided. A three-to-five-minute story is recorded from
a speaker of the regional vernacular and then checked with a group of speakers from the same region
to ensure that the spoken forms are truly representative of that area. The story is then transcribed
and a set of comprehension questions is constructed based on various semantic domains covered in
the text. Normally, a set of fifteen or more questions is initially prepared. Some of the questions will
prove unsuitable – perhaps because the answer is not in focus in the text, or because the question is
confusing to native speakers of the test variety. Unsuitable questions are then deleted from the
preliminary set, leaving a minimum of ten final questions for each RTT. To ensure that measures of
comprehension are based on the subjects’ understanding of the text itself and not on a
misunderstanding of the test questions, these questions must be recorded in the regional variety of
the test subjects. This requires an appropriate dialect version of the questions for each RTT at each
In the RTTs used in this study, test subjects heard the complete story text once, after which the
story was repeated with the inserted test questions. . Each question was followed by a pause to give
the testees the opportunity to respond. Appropriate and correct responses are directly extractable
from the segment of speech immediately preceding the question, such that memory limitations exert
a negligible effect and indirect inference based on the content is not required. Thus, the RTT aims to
be a close reflection of a subject’s comprehension of the text, and by inference, of the language itself,
and not of his or her memory, intelligence, or reasoning. The average or mean of the scores obtained
from subjects at one test location is taken as a numerical indicator of the intelligibility between
In order to ensure that the RTT is a fair test of the intelligibility of the test variety to speakers
from the regions tested, the text is first tested with subjects from the region where the text was
recorded. This initial testing is referred to as the
the subjects to the testing procedure in a context where intelligibility of the dialect is assumed to be
complete since it is the native variety of the test subjects. In addition, hometown testing ensures that
native speakers of the text dialect could accurately answer the comprehension questions used to
assess understanding of the text in nonnative dialect areas. Once a text has been hometown tested
with a minimum of ten subjects who have been able to correctly answer the selected comprehension
questions, with an average score of 90 percent or above, the test is considered validated.
It is possible that a subject may be unable to answer the test questions correctly simply because
he or she does not understand what is expected. This is especially true with unsophisticated subjects
or those unacquainted with test-taking. Therefore, a very short pretest story with four questions is
recorded in the local variety before beginning the actual testing. The purpose of this pretest is to
teach the subject what is expected according to the RTT procedures. If the subject is able to answer
the pretest questions, it is assumed that he or she would serve as a suitable subject. Each subject then
participates in the HTT in his or her native variety before participating in RTTs in nonnative
varieties. Occasionally, even after the pretest, a subject fails to perform adequately on an already
validated HTT. Performances of such subjects are eliminated from the final evaluation, the
assumption being that uncontrollable factors unrelated to the intelligibility of speech forms are
skewing such test results. In this study, subjects performing at levels of less than 80 percent on their
HTT were eliminated from further testing.
When speakers of one linguistic variety have had no previous contact with that represented by
the recorded text, test scores of the subjects from the test point tend to be more similar – especially
when the scores are in the higher ranges. Such consistent scores are often interpreted to be closer
reflections of the inherent intelligibility between speech forms. If the sample of subjects (a minimum
of ten) accurately represents the speech community being tested in terms of the variables affecting
intelligibility, and the RTT scores show such consistency, increasing the number of subjects should
not significantly increase the range of variation of the scores.
However, when some subjects have had significant previous contact with the speech form
recorded on the RTT, while others have not, the scores usually vary considerably, reflecting the
degree of learning that has gone on through contact. For this reason, it is important to include a
measure of dispersion which reflects the extent to which the range of scores varies from the mean –
the standard deviation. On an RTT with 100 possible points (that is, 100%) a standard deviation of
more than 12–15 is considered high. If the standard deviation is relatively low, say 10 and below,
and the mean score for subjects from the selected test point is high, the implication is that the
community as a whole probably understands the test variety rather well, either because the variety
in the RTT is inherently intelligible or because the variety has been acquired rather consistently and
uniformly throughout the speech community. If the standard deviation is low and the mean RTT
score is also low, the implication is that the community as a whole understands the test variety
rather poorly and that regular contact has not facilitated learning of the test variety to any significant
extent. If the standard deviation is high, regardless of the mean score, one implication is that some
subjects have learned to comprehend the test variety better than others. In this last case, inherent

High standard deviations can result from other causes such as inconsistencies under the
circumstances of test administration and scoring, or differences in attentiveness or intelligence of the
subjects. Researchers involved in recorded-text testing need to be aware of the potential for skewed
results due to such factors, and to control for them as much as possible through careful test
Questionnaires administered at the time of testing can help researchers discover which factors
are significant in promoting contact, which facilitates acquired intelligibility. Travel to or extended
stay in other dialect regions, intermarriage between dialect groups, or contacts with schoolmates
from other dialect regions are examples of the types of contact that can occur.
In contrast to experimentally controlled testing in a laboratory or classroom situation, the
results of field-administered methods such as the RTT cannot be completely isolated from potential
biases. Recorded texts and test questions will vary in terms of their relative difficulty and complexity,
or of the clarity of the recording. Comparisons of RTT results from different texts need to be made
cautiously. It is therefore recommended that results from RTTs not be interpreted in terms of fixed
numerical thresholds, but rather be evaluated in light of other indicators of intelligibility such as
lexical similarity, dialect opinions, and reported patterns of contact and communication. In general,
however, RTT mean scores of around 80 percent or higher with accompanying low standard
deviations are usually taken to indicate that respondents of the test point dialect display adequate
understanding of the variety represented by the recording. Conversely, RTT means below 60 percent
are interpreted to indicate inadequate intelligibility.
